examples: Kyoto has a charm all its own.
We offer service you can only get at our store.
I'm always amazed by ideas that only he could come up with.
Please be sure to enjoy an experience you can only have here.
You can feel the changing of the four seasons that is unique to Japan.
Agility that only a small business can have is our strength.
fields.explain:
Used to praise and emphasize “the quality found only in/belonging only to” N.
Avoid using it with strongly negative content; if used, it becomes sarcastic and needs a clear context.
Suitable for headlines, brochures, reviews and PR articles.
The form “N ならではだ” is concise and gives strong emphasis.

• “～ならでは” emphasizes the uniqueness/distinctive character found only in N; it praises and highlights.
• Usually used in a positive context: strengths, identity, competitive advantages.
• N is usually a place name, an organization, a store, a person with their own style, regional culture or a special material.
• It has a strong advertising/promotional nuance, but is also used in everyday conversation to give praise.
fields.notes:
• Can imply a comparison with other places/targets without stating the comparison directly.
• In PR, it often appears with positive vocabulary: 体験・魅力・景観・味・香り・強み・こだわり・サービス.
• Sarcastic use: 文句ならではの多さ (the “characteristic” amount of complaints of ~), but context is needed so the listener understands it as sarcasm.
mistakes: Using it for a directly negative meaning → the nuance is off; if you must, there should be a clear sarcastic/metaphorical context.
Confusing it with “だけの”: “ならでは” stresses “uniqueness/distinctiveness”; “だけの” indicates quantity/limitation.
Dropping “の” when modifying a noun: you need “ならではの N”.
Wrong order: “N のならでは” is incorrect; the correct form is “N ならでは（の）”.

rows: <ruby>職人<rt>しょくにん</rt></ruby>ならではの<ruby>技<rt>わざ</rt></ruby>
N だけの／N ならではの vs N <ruby>固有<rt>こゆう</rt></ruby>の・<ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の
<ruby>固有<rt>こゆう</rt></ruby>の/<ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の are more neutral descriptive vocabulary
<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby><ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>文化<rt>ぶんか</rt></ruby>
Does not imply “only N has it”
これこそ<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ
ここにしかない<ruby>景色<rt>けしき</rt></ruby>

examples: Could you give us your impressions, even in just a word?
I would be glad if I could be of help, even a little.
You must not waste even a single yen.
Please let me help, even if it's just a little.
Please accept this, even if it is only a small token of my feelings.
If anything is unclear, please do not hesitate to ask.
fields.explain:
Polite/courteous; used a lot in letters and formal conversation when making a suggestion or request.
Implies that the speaker lowers the level of expectation so that the listener can accept easily.
Not used directly after the dictionary form of a verb; nominalize it instead: 参加→参加、手伝う→手伝い.
With quantities, it is usually a small amount; avoid using it with large amounts, as that goes against the “minimum” nuance.

• States a minimum: “even just … ”, expressing a minimal concession or the hope that at least the smallest amount will be accepted.
• A humble offer/suggestion: offering to help “at least …”, avoiding a sense of pressure.
• Emphasizes smallness and limitation: often used with words for small amounts (一言・一円・少し・気持ちなど).
• The phrase なんなりとも has the broader meaning “anything at all”, different from the “minimum” meaning.
fields.notes:
• In formal written language, なりとも sounds more courteous than ～でも/だけでも.
• Often used with abstract nouns: 気持ち・援助・情報・意見・協力.
• Business set phrases: なんなりとも＋お申し付けください／お尋ねください.
• Goes well with せめて for emphasis: せめて一言なりとも.
mistakes: Using it after an ordinary verb: × 手伝うなりとも → ○ 手伝いなりとも.
Using it with a large amount gives the wrong nuance: × 一万円なりともあげる → use it with a small amount such as 一円/少し.
Confusing なんなりとも with “minimum”: なんなりとも = “any”, different from “at least”.
Confusing it with ～でも: the JLPT often tests the polite nuance and the “minimum level”.

rows: Neutral; does not stress the “minimum” as strongly as なりとも.
<ruby>一言<rt>ひとこと</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して。
Close in meaning; せめて expresses the feeling “at least”.
せめて<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いだけでもしたい。
なんなりと/なんなりとも
Set phrase meaning “as you wish”, not “minimum”.
なんなりとお<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>付<rt>つ</rt></ruby>けください。
わずかでも/<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しでも
Purely adverbial; lacks the stylized nuance of なりとも.
<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しでも<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けたい。

examples: I saw the sea for the first time at the age of fifty.
I finally passed on my third try.
It is a theory that only an expert can understand.
He is a doctor and also a writer.
Even today, there are still countless problems that must be solved.
There are feelings you only understand once you become a parent.
fields.explain:
Formal/written language; creates an emphatic, slightly dramatic impression.
With “age/number of times”: expresses that something was achieved late or after many tries; often used with ようやく/初めて.
With “limitation”: usually has初めて to emphasize “only when… ”.
With “AにしてB”: the two nouns should be of equal/impressive status.

• Point in time/age: emphasizes lateness, rarity or surprise (五十歳にして, 三度目にして).
• Limitation of ability: emphasizes “only at that level/position is it possible” (専門家にして初めて～).
• Two roles at once: formal written language describing a person/institution with two roles (医師にして作家).
• The form にしてなお adds a concessive meaning = “even now, still…”.
fields.notes:
• “AにしてB” is often used in titles/introductions: 世界的ピアニストにして作曲家のX氏.
• “Nにして初めて” is an almost fixed formula in academic books and essays.
• “今日にしてなお/今にしてなお” is used in newspapers to emphasize “still… even now”.
• Avoid overusing it in everyday conversation, as it sounds stilted.
mistakes: Confusing it with になって: にして has a formal nuance and a sense of surprise; になって is neutral.
Using “AにしてB” for two nouns that do not match → sounds forced: × 学生にして社長 (except in special cases).
Dropping “初めて” in the limitation pattern weakens the meaning: 専門家にして理解できる → still correct, but exams usually prefer “初めて”.
Using it directly with a verb: にして attaches to nouns; nominalize when needed.

rows: Spoken language; lacks the formal/emphatic nuance of にして.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>になって<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かった。
Neutral expression; にして is formal and concise.
<ruby>医師<rt>いし</rt></ruby>で<ruby>作家<rt>さっか</rt></ruby>でもある。
Emphasizes the subject; does not mean “only when/not until”.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>鍵<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>だ。
Indicates place/setting; lacks the three versatile meanings of にして.
<ruby>歴史<rt>れきし</rt></ruby>において<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>。

examples: Whether you are a student or a working adult, time management is important.
Whether you go or not, please let us know early.
Whether it is expensive or cheap, you should check the quality.
Rain or snow, the game will be held as scheduled.
Whether or not you have experience, we welcome your application.
Even if it's a joke, there are things you can say and things you can't.
fields.explain:
A and B should be the same part of speech and play the same grammatical role. After AにしろBにしろ there is usually a comma, followed by a general concluding clause.
Suffix particles: は/も/など are often attached after the whole phrase to make it the topic/for emphasis. Example:時間にしろお金にしろは大切だ。
Nuance: neutral → slightly colloquial; used in stating rules, advice and judgments. For a more formal tone, use ～にせよ／～であれ.
Used with question words to cover a wide scope:誰にしろ、どこにしろ、いつにしろ…
Single form “～にしろ”: has the concessive meaning “even if… still…”. Example:少し無理 にしろ、挑戦する価値はある。 (Even if it is a bit too much, it is worth trying.)
Often used with connecting words that add emphasis: たとえ、いずれ、結局など.

Meaning: “Whether it is A or B, (the conclusion) is the same”, “Regardless of A or B…”. Emphasizes that both options (usually of the same category or opposite in meaning) lead to the same evaluation/decision in the second clause.
• Character: has a generalizing nuance, close to neutral spoken language. Compared with ～にせよ／～であれ, ～にしろ is softer and more everyday.
• The following structure is usually an evaluation, position, request or rule: ～べきだ／～なければならない／～たい／～は変わらない…
• Combines naturally with pairs of opposites (高い/安い、賛成/反対、有無、有/無、行く/行かない…).
• Can be used with question words: 誰にしろ／どこにしろ／いつにしろ… meaning “no matter who/where/when”.
• たとえ can be added to strengthen the concessive nuance: たとえAにしろBにしろ…
• The single form “～にしろ” is also used like “even if... ”, close to ～にしても/～ても.
fields.notes:
• Form: ～にせよ is the original formal form; ～にしろ is the colloquialized form (the command form “しろ” of する), but in this pattern it has no command meaning.
• Naturalness: with na-adjectives, spoken language usually uses them directly: 便利にしろ不便にしろ; in serious written language, である can be used.
• Particle position: は/も/など can be placed after the whole phrase to mark the topic/for emphasis. Avoid inserting case particles after each element unless the structure clearly allows it.
• Three or more items can be listed: AにしろBにしろCにしろ…, but keep it short to avoid confusion.
• The second clause should be a general clause that applies to all options; avoid information that is true for only one side.
• Common combinations: 賛成にしろ反対にしろ／有利にしろ不利にしろ／行くにしろ行かないにしろ／多いにしろ少ないにしろ.
mistakes: Confusing it with the command “～にしろ!”: 静かにしろ (Be quiet!) is not the listing pattern, but the command “しろ” of する + the state marker “に”. Do not confuse it with AにしろBにしろ.
Mixing parts of speech: both parts must be the same type. Incorrect: 学生にしろ来ないにしろ…; Correct: 学生にしろ社会人にしろ… or 行くにしろ行かないにしろ…
Inappropriate suffix particle: avoid inserting を right after each element. Place the particle after the whole phrase: 時間にしろお金にしろは大切だ。 (Instead of ×時間にしろお金にしろを…)
Choosing a second clause that does not cover both: the conclusion must be true for both A and B. If it is true for only one side, use a different structure.
Register: formal writing (reports, JLPT reading essays) should prefer ～にせよ／～であれ to suit the context.
Negative forms: with verbs use V-ないにしろ; with i-adjectives use A-くないにしろ. Example: 参加しないにしろ、連絡して。/ 寒くないにしろ、上着を持っていけ。
Past tense: V-たにしろ／V-なかったにしろ can be used to cover the past. Example: 行ったにしろ行かなかったにしろ、報告して。

Distinction trap with ～にかかわらず／～を問わず: these two patterns do not require listing contrasting items; they are used to cover an entire range (年齢、性別…). ～にしろ～にしろ leans toward giving representative/opposite examples.

rows: Whether A or B, the conclusion is the same
Neutral spoken language; often used with opposites/items of the same category.
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>にしろ<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>にしろ、<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
More formal, leaning toward written language/speeches.
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>にせよ、<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>してください。
Similar to “regardless of A or B”
Most formal; usually used with nouns/technical terms.
<ruby>貧富<rt>ひんぷ</rt></ruby>であれ、<ruby>法<rt>ほう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>では<ruby>平等<rt>びょうどう</rt></ruby>だ。
A single concession; AにしてもBにしても also exists but is less common and weaker in the “regardless” sense.
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いにしても、<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Does not list contrasting items; used for a single condition.
Formal; usually used with nouns/range expressions (<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>性別<rt>せいべつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>…).
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず、<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>する。

examples: The problem is not limited to schools; it is also spreading to families.
His research influenced not only academia but also industry.
Its popularity was not limited to the capital region; it also spread to the provinces.
The effects of global warming are not limited to environmental problems; they also deal a blow to the economy.
This method does not stop at theory; it is also applied in practice.
The effects of the loss of tropical rainforests are not limited to the surrounding areas; they extend to the entire planet.
fields.explain:
Formal; used in reports and presentations; adds weight to an argument.
Suitable when A is a subset and B is a larger set on the same classification axis.
Avoid using it for everyday listing or for targets that have no inclusive relationship.

Expresses that something is not confined to the scope of A but extends to B (a wider one). It highlights the quality of “going beyond the boundary”, so it suits contexts of scale/impact.
• The second clause often has words of breadth/spread: 全体に・広く・多方面に・世界に.
• Common content: damage, influence, popularity, fields of application, significance.
• Can be combined with figures/levels to emphasize the degree of expansion.
fields.notes:
• Effective when combined with a corresponding phrase: Aにとどまらず、Bにまで～／Bにも～。
• Strong as a modifier: ～にとどまらない影響／意味／範囲／成果.
• In headlines: “～、国内にとどまらず” quickly conveys the wide spread.
mistakes: The second clause does not expand → the “going beyond the scope” logic is lost.
Using it for two items of the same level with no inclusion (A and B are siblings, not “outside A”).
Confusing it with “に限らず”: a distinction trap between “inclusion/spreading” vs “universality”.

rows: Not only A but also B
Does not stress “going beyond the scope”; widely used
AだけでなくBも<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Stresses universality across the whole category; not “spreading”
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らず<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>も<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>ぶ。
Close in meaning, but lacks the “not stopping at” nuance
<ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>のみならず<ruby>経済<rt>けいざい</rt></ruby>も～。
Written variant with an active nuance
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>理論<rt>りろん</rt></ruby>にとどめず<ruby>実践<rt>じっせん</rt></ruby>へ。

fields.meaning: No need to…, not necessary to…
examples: There is no need to worry about that matter.
There is no need for you to go to the trouble of coming.
I'm no match for him in ability, but I make up for it with effort.
A detailed explanation is unnecessary. I will just state the main points.
There is plenty of time, so there is no need to hurry.

A: I'd like to come and return the umbrella I borrowed the other day. Would today be convenient for you?
B: Oh, there's no need for that. Please bring it the next time you come.
fields.explain:
Often used in notices/messages/polite refusals: お礼には及びません.
The meaning “cannot compare with” has a modest nuance or expresses an objective evaluation.
Suitable for written language and formal speeches; also used in polite conversation.

• No need/not necessary to: used when an action is superfluous or unnecessary. Example: 連絡するには及ばない.
• Cannot compare with: expresses inferiority in ability or degree. Example: 経験では彼には及ばない.
• Nuance: more formal and polite than ～までもない/～なくてもいい.
fields.notes:
• Fixed keigo expressions: ご心配には及びません／お礼には及びません.
• In the “no need” meaning, the subject is usually a future/proposed action; avoid using it for something that has already happened.
• The “cannot compare with” meaning is often used with nouns referring to people/abilities: 速度・経験・実力＋には及ばない.
mistakes: Confusing the meaning with ～に及ぶ (extend/reach) because of the similar form.
Missing “に”: incorrect “心配するは及ばない” (correct: 心配するには及ばない).
Using it for something already done in the past: ×もう説明したから説明するには及ばない (a time contradiction).
Confusing it with ～には当たらない: “not worth …” (evaluation) is different from “no need to …” (necessity).

rows: Close to the meaning “no need”; ～には<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない is more formal.
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>するまでもない。
Close to “cannot compare with”, leaning toward rivalry/competition.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>さにかなわない。
Completely different meaning; be careful not to confuse it with ～には<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない.
<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>広範囲<rt>こうはんい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ぶ。

examples: Unlike my quiet father, my mother talks a lot.
In contrast to the calm first half, the second half was full of upheaval.
Compared with the mild south side, the wind is cold on the north side.
In contrast to my senior's clear presentation, my main points were vague.
In contrast to last year, which went well, this year growth has stalled.
fields.explain:
Has a strong evaluative nuance; used in criticism/comments.
Not used to compare objective figures; when you need to be neutral, switch to “に比べて/に対して”.
The second clause usually states a clear contrast and is the focus of the statement.

“～にひきかえ” states a clear contrast between A and B, together with the speaker's evaluation. Often used to emphasize opposition in quality/personality/situation between two sides that can be placed on the same axis of comparison.
• The two parts should be naturally comparable: weather on one day vs another, one person vs another, the previous part vs this part.
• Works well when you want to express a subjective impression, not just numerical information.
• Easily combined with contrastive evaluation phrases: ～のに対し／一方で (when you need to be more neutral).
fields.notes:
• Rhetorically effective when A is positive and B negative (or vice versa) to create a sharp contrast.
• Use inversion of A/B to change the focus of emphasis.
• In writing, placing a comma after “にひきかえ” helps separate the argument: ～にひきかえ、～。
mistakes: Missing “の” when A is a clause/adjective: × 暑かったにひきかえ → 〇 暑かったのにひきかえ.
Using it for comparing figures → unsuitable; use “に比べて”.
The two parts are not on the same axis of comparison → the sentence is forced/hard to understand.

rows: Neutral, can be used for figures
<ruby>昨年<rt>さくねん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて5％<ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>。
Aは<ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>、Bは<ruby>減<rt>げん</rt></ruby>なのに<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して。
Same subject, not two different targets
<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かな<ruby>反面<rt>はんめん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で～。

examples: This year there are even more typhoons than usual.
Today I'm calmer than ever.
She is putting even more passion into her work than before.
Life is more important than anything else.
With the weak yen, the tailwind for exports is stronger than ever.
fields.explain:
Formal/rhetorical; expresses a strong increase, an appeal, or emphasis on a topic.
Used adverbially before adjectives/verbs; rarely used directly before a noun (needs の to act as a modifier).
Choose a natural reference point:去年/以前/例年/従来/他人/いつも.

Expresses that the current degree is higher than a reference point (the past, other people, a standard). Has an emphatic/rhetorical tone and often appears in speeches, commentary and news headlines.
• Suitable for: degrees of emotion/qualities (重要/深刻/厳しい/高い/強い/多い).
• Suggests a “significant increase”, not just a small measurable difference.
• Can be combined with intensifying adverbs: さらに/一層/ますます (avoid excessive redundancy).
fields.notes:
• Used with question words for very strong emphasis: 何/誰/いつにもまして.
• In corporate speeches: 「安心・安全を何にもまして最優先します」。
• Rare as a modifier: 例年にもましての猛暑（written language/headlines).
mistakes: Using it for purely numerical differences → use “より/以上に”.
No clear reference point (when not using a question word) → the sentence is vague.
Confusing it with “にも劣らず” (no less than) → the meaning goes in the opposite direction.

rows: Neutral; lacks the “more than ever” nuance
<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>より<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>予想<rt>よそう</rt></ruby><ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
ますます／<ruby>一段<rt>いちだん</rt></ruby>と
No specific reference point for comparison
ますます<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>になる。
<ruby>以前<rt>いぜん</rt></ruby>にも<ruby>増<rt>ま</rt></ruby>して<ruby>厳<rt>きび</rt></ruby>しい。
